subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: In a Melbourne primary school Ms Clarke had taught the class a drill: say "I need help" and point at one adult by name. On Thursday at lunch Zeynep saw two bigger boys take Hiroshi's cap and toss it over the fence while Hiroshi stood with fists tight. A crowd of children watched. Zeynep's heart thumped. "Tattletale" was a word Zeynep had heard before. But Zeynep pointed at the duty teacher and called, "Mr Ellis, I need help, Hiroshi's cap!" He came at once, fetched the cap and stayed with Hiroshi for the rest of lunch. Later Ms Clarke thanked Zeynep and spoke with the two boys.

qa.q: What did Ms Clarke teach the class to say?
qa.a: Ms Clarke taught the class to say "I need help" and point at one adult by name.

qa.q: What was Zeynep feeling before calling Mr Ellis?
qa.a: Zeynep felt nervous, with a thumping heart, and worried about being called a tattletale, but chose to ask for help anyway.

qa.q: What made Zeynep's request work so quickly?
qa.a: Zeynep pointed at a specific adult, Mr Ellis, by name and said exactly what was wrong, so he knew who was needed and why.

qa.q: How might Hiroshi have felt when Mr Ellis came and stayed for the rest of lunch?
qa.a: Hiroshi probably felt relieved and less alone; standing with tight fists before shows how upset and powerless Hiroshi had been.

grounding: A child learns that getting help is caring, not tattling, by practising "I need help" and pointing at one specific adult.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage: Mrs Kaur had a poster on the wall: "Getting help is caring, not tattling." At break Vikas saw a group of older boys tip Tarun's tiffin into the bin while a ring of children watched and giggled. Tarun stood still, lips tight. Vikas's knees felt weak. He walked to the staffroom door and said, "Mrs Kaur, I need help. Tarun's tiffin is in the bin and the big boys are standing over him." Mrs Kaur put down her tea and followed him at once, sent the boys to the head, and took Tarun to the canteen for a fresh sandwich. That afternoon she also phoned Tarun's family.

qa.q: What did Vikas say at the staffroom door?
qa.a: Vikas said, "Mrs Kaur, I need help. Tarun's tiffin is in the bin and the big boys are standing over him."

qa.q: What might Vikas be feeling as his knees go weak before speaking to Mrs Kaur?
qa.a: Vikas feels frightened and torn about getting involved, but the poster's idea that help is caring pushes him to speak.

qa.q: What turning point made Vikas's help effective?
qa.a: Vikas walked to Mrs Kaur, named her and described exactly what was happening, so she could act at once.

qa.q: What might Tarun have felt when Mrs Kaur arrived and took him to the canteen?
qa.a: Tarun probably felt relieved and cared for, after standing still with tight lips while others giggled.

grounding: A child learns that getting help from a teacher is caring, not tattling, by saying "I need help" to one specific adult.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
I sit two rows behind Wasim in Class 6, so I saw it all, though I can't say what he was thinking.
At lunch, three older boys took Usha's water bottle and kept throwing it over her head. She was jumping, going red. Lots of us laughed a bit. Wasim didn't. He looked around, then went straight to the staffroom door.
I followed to see. He knocked and said to Mr Rao, very clearly, “Sir, I need help. Usha is being troubled near the tap.” He pointed at the tap.
Mr Rao came out at once, got the bottle back, and took the three boys inside. He called Usha's mother that afternoon.
Later someone said, “Tattletale.” Wasim just said, “She needed help,” and sat down.

qa.q: What did the older boys take from Usha?
qa.a: They took Usha's water bottle.

qa.q: What did Wasim's clear words at the staffroom suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: He seemed determined and calm, clear that asking for help was the right thing to do.

qa.q: Why was Wasim's way of asking for help effective?
qa.a: He went to one specific adult, said "I need help" and pointed to the place, so Mr Rao could act at once.

qa.q: How might Usha have felt when Mr Rao came out?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and less alone, after being humiliated while others laughed.

grounding: A classmate describes a child going to one specific teacher and saying he needs help, showing that telling is caring, not tattling.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Monday: In the school's safety class, Ms Pinto asked, “Is telling a tattle or caring?” Maria wasn't sure. Ms Pinto made each child say, out loud, “I need help,” and name one grown-up they would go to. Maria chose Joy aunty, the bus attendant.
Wednesday: On the bus home, two boys pulled Pallavi's plait and grabbed her tiffin. Pallavi started crying. Maria froze. Tattle, said a voice in her head. She did nothing, and felt bad all evening.
Friday: It happened again. Maria's heart pounded. She walked to the front and said, “Joy aunty, I need help. Those boys are hurting Pallavi.” She pointed. Joy aunty moved the boys to the front seat, sat Pallavi beside her, and wrote a note for the principal that same afternoon.

qa.q: Which grown-up did Maria choose?
qa.a: Maria chose Joy aunty, the bus attendant.

qa.q: How did Maria feel on Wednesday evening?
qa.a: She felt bad and guilty for freezing when Pallavi was crying.

qa.q: What helped Maria speak up on Friday?
qa.a: Having practised saying "I need help" and already choosing one specific adult made it easier to act, even with her heart pounding.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt when Joy aunty sat her in front?
qa.a: She probably felt safer and comforted, knowing an adult had noticed and would stop the boys.

grounding: Shows a child who learns that telling is caring, practises saying she needs help, and goes to one chosen adult.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Dhruv, you asked if telling the teacher is snitching. Let me tell you what your Minakshi dadi did when she was your age, in Class 5 in Jabalpur.
There was a girl, Radha, who some older girls kept locking in the storeroom at lunch, for fun. Everybody knew. Everybody thought, not my business, and snitching is bad.
One day I heard her banging on the door. My legs shook. I didn't open it myself; I couldn't reach the latch. I ran to our headmistress, Mrs Dubey, and said, “Ma'am, I need help. Radha is in the storeroom.” I pointed.
She came running and let Radha out. Those girls never did it again.
It wasn't snitching, beta. It was caring.

qa.q: Where did the older girls lock Radha?
qa.a: They locked her in the storeroom.

qa.q: How did young Minakshi feel when she heard Radha banging on the door?
qa.a: She felt scared, since her legs shook, but she cared enough to run for help.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Radha?
qa.a: Minakshi running to Mrs Dubey, saying "I need help" and pointing, which brought an adult who let Radha out.

qa.q: How might Radha have felt when the door opened?
qa.a: She was probably frightened and then deeply relieved to be let out and helped.

grounding: An elder recalls going to one specific adult and saying she needed help for a locked-in girl, which was caring, not tattling.

subtopic: Bystander effect and diffusion of responsibility
passage:
Sports day was loud: drums, whistles, the loudspeaker crackling out names. Behind the stands, Francis sat in the dust holding his ankle while three Class 6 boys laughed and called him a baby.
"Don't go tattling," one of them told Rajni.
Rajni's heart thumped. Last week Ms Kaur had made them practise: pick one grown-up, look at them, say "I need help."
Rajni pushed through the crowd to the first-aid table, stood right in front of Mr D'Souza and said it loudly: "I need help. My friend Francis is hurt behind the stands." She pointed.
Mr D'Souza came at once with an ice pack, sent the older boys away and knelt beside Francis. Later, Ms Kaur squeezed Rajni's shoulder. "That wasn't tattling. That was looking after your friend."

qa.q: What had Ms Kaur made them practise last week?
qa.a: Pick one grown-up, look at them, and say "I need help."

qa.q: How was Rajni feeling when the older boy said "Don't go tattling"?
qa.a: Rajni's heart thumped: she was nervous about being called a tattletale by older boys, but more worried about Francis.

qa.q: Why did going to one specific adult work in the noisy crowd?
qa.a: Standing in front of Mr D'Souza and pointing made the request impossible to miss, so he knew it was his job to act right away.

qa.q: What might it be like for Francis when Mr D'Souza arrives?
qa.a: Francis likely feels relieved and less alone, because an adult looks after his ankle and sends the teasing boys away.

grounding: Shows a child using a practised line to ask one specific adult for help and learning that telling is caring, not tattling.
